transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see us today?

Lately, I feel like my whole sense of whether I’m doing okay depends on keeping my body as lean as possible, and it’s starting to take over my life. It has just become really exhausting to constantly worry about it.
Do you find yourself restricting the amount of food you eat or engaging in excessive exercise to maintain this lean body ideal?

Yes, I've been restricting my food heavily, sometimes just having a plain coffee for breakfast and half a chicken breast for dinner, while also jogging much longer distances. I track every calorie in an app, and if I go over my limit even a little, I feel this intense panic like I've completely lost control.

Do you also experience significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other areas of life due to a fear of gaining weight or becoming 'fat', even when you're already underweight or at a normal weight?

Yes, absolutely—the fear of losing the lean image I've worked so hard for has caused a lot of issues at work and with my family. I've had to cut client meetings short because I get lightheaded, and I avoid business lunches entirely. I've also been turning down family get-togethers because I don't want to deal with everyone commenting on how little I'm eating.
Can you tell me what your current weight is and how it compares to what you consider your ideal weight, or the weight at which you feel you look your best?

I don't really have a specific target weight in mind, but my pants are currently hanging off me and everyone says I look too thin. Even so, I'm terrified of losing my lean image and still feel like I need to tighten up more, constantly checking if my jawline looks sharp enough or if my clothes cling to my waist.
Can you tell me if you have experienced a significant amount of weight loss over the past few months, and if so, what was your weight at its lowest point?

Yes, I've definitely lost a lot of weight over the last few months, to the point where all my clothes are hanging off me. I don't actually know the exact number of my lowest weight, as I try not to focus too much on the specific number on the scale.
Have you noticed any changes in your menstrual cycle, such as irregular periods or a complete stop in menstruation, since you started restricting your food intake and exercising excessively?
Actually, I'm a man, so I don't have a menstrual cycle. I haven't had to deal with anything like that.
Do you often find yourself checking your body in mirrors or reflective surfaces, or do you avoid looking at yourself altogether due to concerns about your appearance?

Yes, I check myself in the mirror constantly, especially in the morning before work or right before I meet with clients. I obsessively check to see if my jawline looks sharp enough and if my shirt clings anywhere around my waist. It feels like my entire success as a person depends on those physical details looking exactly right.
Do you believe that your worth as a person is directly tied to your ability to maintain this lean body image, and that if you were to gain weight, you would be a failure or less worthy?

Yes, absolutely. It really feels like whether I'm a success or a complete failure in life comes down to how sharp my jawline looks or if my shirt clings around my waist. If I were to gain weight and lose this lean image, I'd feel like I've completely lost control and failed, especially when I have to face my clients.

Do you experience any episodes where you feel like you've lost control and eaten more than you intended, followed by feelings of guilt, shame, or the need to compensate through excessive exercise or purging?

No, I don't ever have episodes where I lose control and overeat, and I definitely don't purge. I just strictly limit how much I eat and stick to a very rigid running routine to make sure I keep my weight down.
Have you been using any supplements or steroids to help achieve or maintain your lean body image, or have you been engaging in specific muscle-building exercises?
No, I haven't used any supplements or steroids at all. My exercise is really just focused on running longer distances to stay lean, rather than doing any muscle-building workouts.
Do you believe that others see you as underweight or too thin, or do you think they see you as you see yourself, needing to be even leaner?

My mom, my sister, and the doctors keep telling me that I'm way too thin, and my mom even says I look like I did after a really bad flu years ago. But in my own head, it feels like they are overreacting because I can still go to work and run every day. To me, I still feel like I need to tighten up and get even leaner.

Can you describe in more detail what you mean by 'tightening up' and how you envision your body looking when you've achieved this ideal lean image, considering others' concerns that you're already underweight?

To me, "tightening up" means having a completely flat waist where my shirt doesn't cling at all and keeping a very sharp, defined jawline. Even though my pants are hanging off me and everyone is worried—especially after my fainting spell—it feels like they're overreacting because I can still work and run. In my mind, I still see areas that could be leaner, and I just don't see myself as too thin yet.

Do you believe your body image concerns and the need to be lean are related to a fear of gaining weight or becoming 'fat', or is it more about achieving a specific physical appearance for perceived attractiveness or athletic performance?

It’s actually a mix of both. I get a rush of panic if I even think about eating a pastelito or some arroz con frijoles, worrying it will immediately show up on my stomach and ruin the lean image I've worked so hard for. But at the same time, I have a deep drive to maintain a very sharp, lean look to feel polished for my clients and to avoid feeling like a failure when looking in the mirror.

Do you think your perception of your body and the need to be lean might be distorted, given that others, including your family and doctors, see you as underweight, while you still believe you need to lose more weight?

Honestly, I don't really feel like it's distorted, even though I know there is a disconnect between how I see myself and how others see me. My family and doctors keep warning me that I'm too thin, but to me, it just feels like they are overreacting. Since I'm still able to go to work and do my daily runs, I don't see how things could really be that bad.

Can you explain why you believe your family and doctors are overreacting when they express concern about your weight, despite your acknowledgment that you're able to work and run, which suggests a level of physical capability?

I feel like they're blowing things out of proportion because if my weight were actually dangerous, I wouldn't be able to keep up with my busy sales job or run miles every day. To me, as long as I can still function physically and get my work done, there's no way my condition is as severe as they make it out to be.
Can you think of any situation or event in the past where you felt completely comfortable with your body weight and image, or has the desire to be lean always been a significant concern for you?

This obsession with being lean is actually pretty recent, as I felt much more comfortable with myself before the difficult separation from my wife. Back then, I loved cooking and eating traditional meals like arroz con frijoles and enjoying family gatherings without worrying about my weight at all. This intense focus on my body and tracking food only started building up after the split when I had to adjust to living alone.

Can you clarify if your primary motivation for maintaining this lean body image is more about avoiding the fear of gaining weight and becoming 'fat', or is it predominantly driven by the desire to achieve a specific, idealized physical appearance for attractiveness or success?

It's really a mix of both for me. I get this intense panic that eating a pastelito or some arroz con frijoles will immediately show up on my stomach, but my self-worth is also deeply tied to looking sharp and polished for my clients. To me, feeling successful comes down to having that sharp jawline and a shirt that doesn't cling around my waist.

Can you elaborate on how your recent separation from your wife might be influencing your perception of your body and your intense focus on being lean, considering this obsession started after the split?

The separation left me living alone for the first time, and without the structure of shared family meals, my emotional life felt completely chaotic. Focusing intensely on tracking my food, restricting my meals, and running became my way of regaining a sense of control. I also felt a strong need to "get back in shape" to present a highly polished, sharp image to my clients and potential new partners.

Can you rate, on a scale of 1 to 10, how much your desire to maintain this lean body image is driven by the fear of gaining weight versus the desire to achieve a specific physical appearance for attractiveness or success?

I’d rate them both incredibly high, around an 8 or 9 out of 10, because they feel completely tangled together. The constant panic of gaining weight and having food show up on my stomach is driven by my intense need to maintain a sharp, polished look to feel successful after my separation. Ultimately, looking lean is the only way I feel attractive to potential partners and confident in front of my clients.

Do you think that even if you were to achieve your ideal lean body image, your fears about gaining weight and your self-worth issues would completely resolve, or do you think these concerns would persist in some form?

To be honest, even though my pants are already hanging off me, I still find myself looking in the mirror thinking I need to "tighten up" a bit more. Deep down, I suspect the fear of gaining it back would stay with me, and my self-worth would still feel fragile because the target always seems to move whenever I look at myself.

Can you describe how your body image concerns and fear of gaining weight relate to your sense of identity and self-worth, and whether you believe achieving your ideal lean body image would fundamentally change your self-perception?

My entire self-worth and sense of being a success or failure is completely tied to my physical appearance, like how sharp my jawline looks or if my clothes cling to my waist when meeting clients. Gaining even a little weight makes me panic because I feel I would lose the lean, polished image I've worked so hard for. Ultimately, maintaining this extreme thinness is the only thing that makes me feel like I am doing okay and in control of my life right now.
Can you clarify if your fear of gaining weight is more related to the potential loss of control over your body or the perceived loss of attractiveness and success that comes with it?

It’s really a mix of both. On one hand, keeping a tight grip on my food and running gives me a sense of control when my life feels chaotic after my separation. On the other hand, losing that sharp, polished image feels like I’m failing at my sales job, and both of those outcomes cause me deep anxiety.

Can you tell me if there's ever a moment when your fear of gaining weight and your desire for a lean body image feel like they're not intertwined, or if one ever takes precedence over the other in your thoughts?

No, they feel completely locked together and never really separate. The intense panic I get about gaining weight—like if I even think about eating a pastelito or some arroz con frijoles—is entirely driven by the fear of ruining the sharp, lean image I need to maintain for my self-worth and my clients. Any weight gain feels like an immediate, total failure of my body image, so they always go hand-in-hand.
